q1_issues.issue: 'on the verge of' is a fixed idiom whose literal reading is incoherent for these participants (starvation has no edge), yet the parse mints a physical `verge` entity the text never introduces — exactly the error the idiom rule forbids.

The idiom's complement is unpacked as a bare `(Of sk_verge_1 starvation)`, whereas the instruction set routes of-phrases to `Possession` / `PartOf` / `SubsetOf` / measure / about readings, none of which is a relation between a verge and starvation.
Nothing in the parse records what the sentence actually states — that the cat was close to starving; the locative `(On ...)` asserts a spatial position instead.
Minor: `(Member sk_cat_1 poor)` is left untensed under a past host clause, unlike the appositive rule where a modifier's atom takes the host clause's wrapper.

q2_gaps: imminent / prospective aspect ('on the verge of X', 'about to V') — no operator records that an eventuality is impending but has not occurred
a fixed idiom that takes a complement ('on the verge of <N>') — the idiom rule provides only a single whole-word surface symbol, with no shape for an idiomatic frame carrying an open argument slot
expressive / sympathetic attributive adjective ('the poor cat'), which conveys the speaker's attitude rather than predicating a property of the referent
notes: The cat's typing and modifier follow the rules, but the core predication is unfaithful: it asserts a physical verge and an `Of` link the text never states while omitting the near-starvation the sentence is about. The idiom's argument-taking shape is itself unaddressed, so the gap list explains part of the failure.
